qAndA.answer: They are called vesicles and contain neurotransmitters.
qAndA.question: What are the names of the small bubbles within the axon terminal and what do they contain?

qAndA.answer: Neurotransmitters are only found at the axon terminal.
qAndA.question: Where specifically on a neuron are neurotransmitters found?

qAndA.answer: The receiving cell gets activated. This could lead to a muscle contraction if it's a muscle cell or an action potential if it's another neuron.
qAndA.question: What happens to the receiving cell when the neurotransmitters bind to its receptors?
What type of neuron detects the initial pin prick in the paw?

qAndA.answer: The sensory neuron transmits the pain signal to the spinal cord where it activates a relay neuron, then a motor neuron. This motor neuron signals the muscles in the paw to contract, leading to the withdrawal reflex.
qAndA.question: Why does the paw withdraw after the pin prick?

text_to_speech: In this lesson we will examine how neurons communicate. But to understand how the nervous system works, we have to understand what it does. It is the main communication system for the entire body that controls things like controlling our muscles, our glands - like our sweat glands and hormones, our sensory structures like eyes and ear. But in order to do this they've got to talk to other neurons. The beauty of the nervous system though is that it communicates with our entire body. There's not one part of our body that does not have a nerve going to or from it. So let's take a look at the cells the neurons. They communicate and do things using a combination of electrical and chemical signals. The neuron is made up of three main parts. Left to right, the dendrites. They are the receiving part the axons which carry the impulse. And the axon terminal which sends a signal like a transmission or a cell phone to another cell. The flow always goes towards the axon terminal so that the flow of the impulse always ends at the axon terminal. How does it transmit the signal to another cell like another nerve this happens all of course at the synapse.  The synapse is where one neuron communicates with another cell. The synapse is actually a very small space between the axon terminal of one cell and the receptor portion of a receiving cell. Notice these little bubbles. Those little bubbles as you can see here in this (little bit more specific) diagram, contains the neurotransmitters. Those are called vesicles those bubbles. So these bubbles contain those neurotransmitters actually, are only found at the axon terminal so when an impulse comes down the axon it causes these axon vesicles to migrate to the membrane where we'll release the neurotransmitters into the synapse. Those neurotransmitters combined with the receptors on the receiving cell now when the receiving cell and the receptor and the neurotransmitter come together that causes cell to go to work like contract. Or you know causing our action potential in the next neuron. So, let's put it all together. So here we have a reflex. So let's say, for example, you get a pin stuck in your paw. A sensory neuron located right around here that's going to cause an impulse to be carried to the spinal cord, where the impulse is transmitted to a relay neuron. And that's going to transmit an impulse to a motor neuron. The motor neuron sends an impulse to the muscle causing it to contract. And that's pretty much it. That's how it all comes together. And now I think you know how a neuron transmits information.
